title: When the Signal Drops

patient.name: Mr Lim Teck Soon
patient.presenting_complaint: Comes monthly for wet AMD injections; needs a macular OCT before review, but the first scan looks poor quality

history.hpc: Mr Lim attends for his regular wet AMD follow-up and macular OCT. He says: 'I come every month for the injection, today need do the scan first right?' On the first attempt the scan shows low signal strength and a dark, grainy image. He has a cataract and dry eyes. The OT must troubleshoot to obtain a usable scan.
history.pmhx: Wet AMD (right eye) on anti-VEGF injections. Cataract both eyes. Dry eye disease.
history.social_hx: Lives with daughter. Attends regularly for injections. Non-smoker.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Cataract both eyes and dry ocular surface — both can reduce OCT signal
examination_findings.fundus: Wet AMD changes right eye; OCT needed to assess fluid for treatment decision

investigations.macular_oct: Initial macular OCT showed low signal strength and a grainy image. Troubleshooting performed: cleaned the lens/optics, asked the patient to blink fully to refresh the tear film (and instilled lubricant), optimised focus and centration, and re-acquired. The repeat scan reached adequate signal strength and showed persistent intraretinal/subretinal fluid right eye.
investigations.scan_quality: First attempt poor (low signal); after troubleshooting, adequate signal and clear foveal centration achieved.

diagnosis: A low-quality macular OCT caused by media opacity (cataract) and a poor tear film, resolved by correct troubleshooting to obtain a usable scan showing persistent fluid in wet AMD. The OT competency is recognising poor scan quality and systematically improving it before saving.

immediate: Recognise the low signal strength/grainy image as an inadequate scan, not a true finding
Troubleshoot systematically: clean the instrument optics, ask the patient to blink/instil lubricant to refresh the tear film
Re-optimise focus, centration on the fovea, and alignment, then re-acquire
Confirm the repeat scan reaches adequate signal strength before saving
Document the indication, eye, scan quality, and findings (persistent fluid) for the doctor
Do not save or report the poor-quality scan as the result
follow_up: Doctor to review the fluid status and decide on continuing anti-VEGF treatment
Note in records that media/tear film reduce signal, for future scan planning
patient_education: Explain you need to repeat the scan to get a clear picture, and ask him to blink fully before the scan
Reassure him the repeat is normal and not a problem with his eye
Explain lubricant drops can help the scan quality
Explain the doctor will use the scan to decide on today's treatment

key_points: Confirms the indication (wet AMD follow-up) and eye to scan
Identifies factors that reduce signal (cataract, dry eye)
Confirms the regular injection context relevant to the scan
Explains the procedure and the need to repeat if needed
Recognises the poor-quality scan rather than accepting it as a finding
Troubleshoots systematically (optics, tear film/blink, focus, centration)
Re-acquires and confirms adequate signal strength before saving
Documents indication, eye, scan quality, and findings
Understands media opacity and tear film can degrade OCT signal
Distinguishes an artefact/poor scan from a true pathological finding
Recognises persistent fluid on the corrected scan
Knows the OT role is acquisition/quality control, not treatment
Obtains a usable, quality-checked scan after troubleshooting
Does not save/report the poor-quality scan as the result
Documents the scan quality and findings clearly
Explains the repeat to the patient and reassures him
